text:
Investing $100 a month sounds too small to matter, until you see what it does through a bad year. Dev put $100 a month into an S&P 500 index fund in January 2000, one of the worst starting dates in modern market history, and watched his account fall below what he had put in, not once but twice. He never stopped. Twenty-five years later he had put in $30,000 and his account held about $146,000.

Two friends started with the same $100. Cora waited for the dust to settle and began in 2003, finishing about $27,700 behind Dev. Pete started the same day Dev did, sold at the end of 2008, and finished about $134,000 behind without making a single bad trade. Same $100. Same fund. Three completely different lives. Here is the real math behind why.

But the numbers hold an uncomfortable surprise. For Dev's first ten years, a plain 2% savings account would have beaten the stock market, about $13,300 against $12,634. More than 90% of what he ended up with arrived after the point where the plan looked like a failure.

In this video: what Dev's account looked like at its worst, what he was really holding while the balance was falling, why a crash lets the same $100 buy more shares, how Lila, who started at the 2009 bottom, still finished with less than half of Dev's total, the moment Pete turned a temporary loss into a permanent one, how a 1% fund fee takes about $19,000 from the same $100, where your first $100 should go, how to find it in forgotten subscriptions, the one kind of money that should never go into stocks, why $146,000 is a start and not a retirement, and the one sentence to write down before the next crash.

Figures come from the calendar-year returns of the S&P 500 with dividends included, spread evenly across each year, and are not adjusted for inflation. Real results would differ somewhat. This is a history lesson, not a forecast. This video is for education and entertainment only and is not financial advice.

text:
Municipal bond interest is free of federal income tax. But when the IRS tests whether your Social Security is taxable, that interest is counted.

• IRS Publication 915: half your benefits + all your other income, including tax-exempt interest
• Our 2026 example: a married couple, both 65+, with $48,000 of Social Security and a $40,000 pension
• Add $10,000 of muni interest and $8,500 more of their benefits becomes taxable
• Their federal tax rises about $850

Hold muni bonds? Count that interest when you check your combined income.

In this video, Logical Money explains 20+ essential stock market terms through simple explanations, relatable examples, and practical comparisons that make investing easier to understand.

Whether you're a beginner learning the stock market basics or an investor looking to better understand stock valuations, dividends, index funds, and trading strategies, this guide will help you make sense of the terminology used in the US stock market and apply it to real-world investing.

WHAT YOU'LL LEARN:
1. Stock Valuation: Share Price, Market Capitalization (Market Cap), Earnings Per Share (EPS), Price-to-Earnings Ratio (P/E Ratio), and Intrinsic Value.
2. Stock Price Movements: Supply and Demand, Investor Expectations, and Market Volatility.
3. Buying and Selling Stocks: Bid Price, Ask Price, Bid-Ask Spread, Market Orders, Limit Orders, and Liquidity.
4. Investment Returns: Capital Gains, Dividends, and Dividend Yield — including why a high dividend yield can sometimes be a warning sign.
5. Investing Strategies: Diversification, Index Funds, the S&P 500, Exchange-Traded Funds (ETFs), Multibagger Stocks, and Dollar-Cost Averaging (DCA).
6. You'll also discover why a low P/E ratio doesn't always mean a stock is undervalued, why profitable companies can experience falling share prices, how trading costs affect your investments, and why investing in an S&P 500 index fund is different from picking individual stocks.

By the end, you'll have a clearer understanding of the investing terminology used by financial analysts, brokerage platforms, and Wall Street professionals — without needing a finance degree.
